sections.title: Matter and how it is classified
sections.html:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Chemistry sorts it in two ways: by its state and by its composition.

States of matter

StateShapeVolumeParticles
SolidFixedFixedPacked tightly, vibrate in place
LiquidTakes the container's shapeFixedClose together, slide past each other
GasFills the containerFills the containerFar apart, move fast and freely

Classifying by composition

  • Pure substance: fixed composition. Either an element (one kind of atom, e.g. O₂, Fe) or a compound (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, e.g. H₂O, NaCl).
  • Mixture: two or more substances physically mixed, in any ratio.
    • Homogeneous (a solution): the same all the way through, e.g. salt water, air, brass.
    • Heterogeneous: you can see different parts, e.g. sand in water, granite, oil and water.

Mixtures are separated by physical methods: filtration, distillation, evaporation, chromatography. Compounds can only be broken down by chemical reactions.

Properties and changes

  • Physical property: observed without changing what the substance is (colour, melting point, density). A physical change keeps the identity: melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper.
  • Chemical property: how it reacts (flammability, reacting with acid). A chemical change makes new substances: burning, rusting, cooking an egg. Signs: gas given off, colour change, precipitate, heat or light.
  • Intensive properties do not depend on the amount (density, temperature, boiling point). Extensive properties do (mass, volume).

Changes of state (melting, boiling, condensing) are physical changes, even though they look dramatic.

checks.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
checks.x: Rusting makes a new substance (iron oxide). The others keep the same substance.

checks.q: Salt water is best classified as a:
checks.x: It is uniform throughout and the salt-to-water ratio can vary, so it is a homogeneous mixture (a solution).

checks.q: Which property is intensive?
checks.x: Density is the same for a small or large sample. Mass, volume and length depend on the amount.

Temperature

\[T(\text{K}) = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273.15 \qquad T(^\circ\text{F}) = 1.8\,T(^\circ\text{C}) + 32\]

Density = mass ÷ volume, usually in g/mL or g/cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³).

Significant figures

  1. All non-zero digits count: 4.56 has 3.
  2. Zeros between non-zero digits count: 1005 has 4.
  3. Leading zeros never count: 0.0045 has 2.
  4. Trailing zeros count only if there is a decimal point: 2.50 has 3; 2500 has 2 (write 2.50 × 10³ for 3).
  5. Exact numbers (counted items, defined values like 1 m = 100 cm) have unlimited significant figures.

Multiply or divide: the answer has as many significant figures as the measurement with the fewest sig figs. Add or subtract: the answer has as many decimal places as the measurement with the fewest decimal places.

WorkedWorked example: rounding results

  • 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6 (2 sig figs, from 2.5).
  • 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = 31.123 → 31.1 (1 decimal place, from 18.0).

Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated results are to each other. Results can be precise but not accurate.

sections.title: Unit conversions (dimensional analysis)
sections.html:
Multiply the starting quantity by conversion factors (fractions equal to 1) arranged so the unwanted units cancel.

\[\text{given} \times \frac{\text{wanted unit}}{\text{given unit}} = \text{answer}\]
  1. Write down the given quantity with its unit.
  2. Choose a factor with the given unit on the bottom.
  3. Chain factors until only the wanted unit is left.
  4. Check that the units cancel and the size of the answer makes sense.

WorkedWorked example: speed

Convert 65 km/h to m/s.

\[65\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}\times\frac{1000\,\text{m}}{1\,\text{km}}\times\frac{1\,\text{h}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 18\,\text{m/s}\]

WorkedWorked example: density as a conversion factor

What volume does 25.0 g of mercury occupy? (density 13.6 g/mL)

\[25.0\,\text{g}\times\frac{1\,\text{mL}}{13.6\,\text{g}} = 1.84\,\text{mL}\]

Squared and cubed units

Cube (or square) the whole factor, numbers included:

\[1\,\text{m}^3 = (100\,\text{cm})^3 = 10^6\,\text{cm}^3 \qquad 1\,\text{L} = 1000\,\text{cm}^3 = 1\,\text{dm}^3\]

The most common slip is cubing only the unit: 1 m³ is not 100 cm³, it is 1 000 000 cm³.

checks.x: (100 cm)³ = 10⁶ cm³.

sections.title: Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass
sections.html:
Dalton's atomic theory: elements are made of atoms; atoms of one element are alike; compounds form when atoms combine in whole-number ratios; reactions rearrange atoms but do not create or destroy them.

ParticleChargeMass (amu)Where
Proton+1≈ 1Nucleus
Neutron0≈ 1Nucleus
Electron−1≈ 0.00055Around the nucleus
  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. It identifies the element.
  • Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. So neutrons = A − Z.
  • Notation: \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\), e.g. \(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}\) has 26 p, 30 n, 26 e⁻.
  • Isotopes: same element (same Z), different numbers of neutrons (different A). They react the same way chemically.
  • Ions: atoms that have gained or lost electrons. Cations are positive (lost e⁻); anions are negative (gained e⁻). Electrons = Z − charge.

Average atomic mass

\[\text{average mass} = \sum (\text{fractional abundance} \times \text{isotope mass})\]

WorkedWorked example: chlorine

Cl-35: 34.969 amu, 75.78 %. Cl-37: 36.966 amu, 24.22 %.

\[0.7578(34.969) + 0.2422(36.966) = 26.50 + 8.953 = 35.45\,\text{amu}\]

Check: the average is closer to 35 because Cl-35 is more common.

checks.q: How many neutrons are in ⁵⁶Fe (Z = 26)?
checks.x: Neutrons = A − Z = 56 − 26 = 30.

checks.q: How many electrons does S²⁻ have? (Z = 16)
checks.x: A 2− ion has gained 2 electrons: 16 + 2 = 18.

checks.q: Isotopes of an element differ in their number of:
checks.x: Isotopes have the same Z (protons) but different numbers of neutrons.

sections.html:
Charges you can read off the periodic table

Most transition metals can form more than one ion, so the charge is shown with a Roman numeral: FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride, FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride. Exceptions with only one charge: Ag⁺, Zn²⁺.

Common polyatomic ions

IonNameIonName

-ate has one more O than -ite (sulfate SO₄²⁻, sulfite SO₃²⁻). per-…-ate has one more O again; hypo-…-ite has one fewer (ClO₄⁻, ClO₃⁻, ClO₂⁻, ClO⁻).

Rules

  1. Name the cation first, then the anion. Monatomic anions end in -ide (chloride, oxide, nitride).
  2. Write formulas so the charges add to zero. The "criss-cross" shortcut: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃.
  3. Put brackets round a polyatomic ion when you need more than one: Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
  4. Hydrates include the water: CuSO₄·5H₂O is copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate (see the Hydrate Formula Lab).

WorkedWorked example: aluminium sulfate

Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻. Lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6: two Al³⁺ (+6) and three SO₄²⁻ (−6). Formula: Al₂(SO₄)₃.

sections.title: The mole and molar mass
sections.html:
A mole is a counting unit: 1 mol contains Avogadro's number of particles.

\[N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{particles/mol}\]

Molar mass (M) is the mass of 1 mol in grams, found by adding the atomic masses from the periodic table: M(H₂O) = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol.

\[n = \frac{m}{M} \qquad N = n \times N_A\]

The road map: grams ⇄ (÷ M / × M) ⇄ moles ⇄ (× NA / ÷ NA) ⇄ particles. You always go through moles.

WorkedWorked example: water

How many molecules, and how many H atoms, are in 10.0 g of water?

\[n = \frac{10.0\,\text{g}}{18.02\,\text{g/mol}} = 0.555\,\text{mol}\]
\[N = 0.555 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 3.34\times10^{23}\ \text{molecules}\]

Each molecule has 2 H atoms: 2 × 3.34 × 10²³ = 6.68 × 10²³ H atoms.

Read the question for molecules or atoms. 1 mol of O₂ is 6.022 × 10²³ molecules but 1.204 × 10²⁴ atoms.

checks.q: The molar mass of CO₂ is about:
How many moles are in 9.80 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98.08 g/mol)?
How many oxygen atoms are in 0.50 mol of O₂?
checks.x: 0.50 mol O₂ × 2 mol O/mol O₂ = 1.0 mol O atoms = 6.0 × 10²³ atoms.

sections.title: Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas
sections.html:
\[\%\ \text{element} = \frac{(\text{atoms in formula})\times(\text{atomic mass})}{\text{molar mass of compound}} \times 100\]

Example: % N in NH₃ = 14.01 / 17.03 × 100 = 82.3 %.

  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms (CH₂O).
  • Molecular formula: the actual numbers of atoms (C₆H₁₂O₆), a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

Finding the empirical formula

  1. Assume 100 g, so the percentages become grams.
  2. Convert grams of each element to moles.
  3. Divide every mole value by the smallest one.
  4. If a ratio is close to x.5, x.33 or x.25, multiply all by 2, 3 or 4 to get whole numbers.
\[\text{molecular formula} = n \times \text{empirical formula},\quad n = \frac{M_\text{molecular}}{M_\text{empirical}}\]

WorkedWorked example: glucose

40.0 % C, 6.71 % H, 53.3 % O; molar mass 180 g/mol.

ElementGramsMoles÷ smallest
C40.040.0/12.01 = 3.331
H6.716.71/1.008 = 6.662
O53.353.3/16.00 = 3.331

Empirical formula CH₂O (30.03 g/mol). n = 180 / 30.03 = 6, so the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.

Don't round 1.5 to 2. A ratio like C₁H₁.₅ means multiply by 2: C₂H₃.

checks.q: The empirical formula of benzene, C₆H₆, is:
checks.x: Divide both subscripts by 6: CH.

sections.title: Writing and balancing chemical equations
sections.html:
A chemical equation shows reactants → products, with states (s), (l), (g), (aq). Atoms are conserved, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides.

How to balance

  1. Write correct formulas. Never change subscripts, only coefficients.
  2. Balance elements that appear in only one compound on each side first.
  3. Leave H and O (and any free element like O₂) until last.
  4. Use the smallest whole-number coefficients, and check every element.

WorkedWorked example: burning propane

C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

  • C: 3 on the left, so 3 CO₂.
  • H: 8 on the left, so 4 H₂O.
  • O on the right: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10, so 5 O₂.

C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O

Types of reaction

TypePatternExample
Combination (synthesis)A + B → AB2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO
DecompositionAB → A + BCaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Combustionfuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂OCH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O
Single displacementA + BC → AC + BZn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
Double displacementAB + CD → AD + CBAgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃

If a coefficient comes out as a fraction (e.g. 13/2 O₂ for C₄H₁₀), multiply every coefficient by 2.

checks.x: Right side has 2 + 2 = 4 O atoms, so 2 O₂.

sections.title: Reaction stoichiometry
sections.html:
The coefficients in a balanced equation give the mole ratio in which substances react and form.

The path: grams of A → (÷ MA) → moles of A → (× mole ratio B/A) → moles of B → (× MB) → grams of B.

WorkedWorked example: CO₂ from propane

C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O. What mass of CO₂ forms from 22.0 g of C₃H₈?

\[22.0\,\text{g C}_3\text{H}_8 \times \frac{1\,\text{mol}}{44.10\,\text{g}} \times \frac{3\,\text{mol CO}_2}{1\,\text{mol C}_3\text{H}_8} \times \frac{44.01\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mol CO}_2} = 65.9\,\text{g CO}_2\]

The mole ratio comes from the coefficients, never from the masses. You cannot go straight from grams of A to grams of B.

checks.q: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. How many moles of NH₃ form from 3.0 mol of H₂ (excess N₂)?
checks.x: 3.0 mol H₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 3 mol H₂) = 2.0 mol.

checks.q: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What mass of O₂ burns 1.00 mol of CH₄?
The mole ratio used in stoichiometry comes from:
o: The coefficients of the balanced equation
checks.x: Coefficients tell you how many moles react with each other.

sections.title: Limiting reactant and percent yield
sections.html:
• The limiting reactant runs out first and decides how much product forms. The other is in excess.
  • Theoretical yield: the most product possible, worked out from the limiting reactant.
  • Actual yield: what you really get in the lab.
\[\%\ \text{yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\]

Method

  1. Convert each reactant to moles.
  2. Work out how much product each one could make (or divide each by its coefficient). The smaller answer marks the limiting reactant.
  3. Use the limiting reactant for the theoretical yield.

WorkedWorked example: making water

2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, with 4.0 g H₂ and 16.0 g O₂. The actual yield is 15.3 g of water.

  • H₂: 4.0 / 2.016 = 1.98 mol → could make 1.98 mol H₂O.
  • O₂: 16.0 / 32.00 = 0.500 mol → could make 1.00 mol H₂O.

O₂ is limiting. Theoretical yield = 1.00 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 18.0 g.

\[\%\ \text{yield} = \frac{15.3}{18.0}\times100 = 85.0\,\%\]

The limiting reactant is not just the one with the smaller mass, or even the fewer moles: you must account for the mole ratio.

checks.q: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. With 3 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂, the limiting reactant is:
checks.x: 2 mol O₂ needs 4 mol H₂, but only 3 mol are present, so H₂ runs out first.

The theoretical yield is calculated from:
checks.x: Product stops forming once the limiting reactant is used up.

sections.title: Solutions: molarity and dilution
sections.html:
A solution is a solute dissolved in a solvent. Concentration is usually given as molarity:

\[M = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{litres of solution}} \qquad n = M \times V\]

WorkedWorked example: making a solution

What mass of NaCl is needed for 250.0 mL of 0.500 M solution?

n = 0.500 mol/L × 0.2500 L = 0.125 mol; mass = 0.125 × 58.44 = 7.31 g. Dissolve it and make up to the mark in a 250 mL volumetric flask.

Dilution

\[M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2\]

The moles of solute stay the same; only the volume changes. Example: to make 500 mL of 0.10 M HCl from 2.0 M stock, V₁ = (0.10 × 500) / 2.0 = 25 mL of stock, made up to 500 mL.

Ion concentrations

Strong electrolytes split fully: 0.10 M CaCl₂ gives 0.10 M Ca²⁺ and 0.20 M Cl⁻.

WorkedWorked example: titration

20.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl exactly neutralises 25.0 mL of NaOH. Find [NaOH].

n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol.

[NaOH] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 M.

Convert mL to L before using M = n/V.

sections.title: Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations
sections.html:
Electrolytes

  • Strong electrolytes split completely into ions: soluble ionic compounds, strong acids, strong bases.
  • Weak electrolytes split only a little: weak acids (CH₃COOH), weak bases (NH₃).
  • Non-electrolytes dissolve as molecules: sugar, ethanol.

Solubility rules

Usually solubleExceptions
All Group 1 and NH₄⁺ compoundsNone
Nitrates, acetates, perchloratesNone
Chlorides, bromides, iodidesAg⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺
SulfatesBa²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ag⁺
Usually insolubleExceptions
Carbonates, phosphatesGroup 1 and NH₄⁺
HydroxidesGroup 1, NH₄⁺; Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺ slightly soluble
SulfidesGroup 1, NH₄⁺, Group 2

A precipitation reaction happens when two solutions mix and an insoluble product forms.

Three ways to write it

  1. Molecular: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
  2. Complete ionic: split every strong electrolyte. Ag⁺ + NO₃⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) + Na⁺ + NO₃⁻
  3. Net ionic: cross out the spectator ions (here Na⁺ and NO₃⁻). Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

Never split solids, liquids, gases or weak electrolytes into ions.

checks.q: Which compound is insoluble in water?
checks.x: Sulfates are soluble except with Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ag⁺.

checks.q: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2 KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2 KNO₃(aq). The spectator ions are:
checks.x: K⁺ and NO₃⁻ appear unchanged on both sides; the net ionic is Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂(s).

checks.q: Which is a weak electrolyte?
checks.x: Acetic acid ionises only slightly. The others split completely.

sections.title: Acid–base and redox reactions
sections.html:
Acids and bases

  • Arrhenius: acids give H⁺ in water; bases give OH⁻.
  • Brønsted–Lowry: acids are proton (H⁺) donors; bases are proton acceptors.
  • Strong acids (learn them): HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄. Strong bases: Group 1 hydroxides, and Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂.
  • Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Net ionic for strong + strong: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

Oxidation numbers

  1. Free element: 0 (Fe, O₂, Cl₂).
  2. Monatomic ion: its charge (Na⁺ = +1).
  3. F is always −1. O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides). H is +1 with non-metals (−1 in metal hydrides).
  4. The sum equals the overall charge: 0 for a compound, the ion's charge for an ion.

WorkedWorked example: oxidation numbers

  • S in H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 → S = +6
  • Mn in MnO₄⁻: Mn + 4(−2) = −1 → Mn = +7
  • Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2 → Cr = +6

Redox

OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons, oxidation number goes up); Reduction Is Gain (oxidation number goes down). The species oxidised is the reducing agent; the species reduced is the oxidising agent.

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): Zn 0 → +2 is oxidised (reducing agent); Cu +2 → 0 is reduced (oxidising agent).

The activity series (Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au) tells you a metal can displace the ion of any metal below it.

checks.q: The oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄ is:
In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is oxidised?
checks.x: Zn loses electrons (0 → +2).

checks.q: Which of these is a strong acid?
checks.x: HNO₃ is on the list of six strong acids; HF is weak.

sections.title: Pressure and the simple gas laws
sections.html:
Pressure = force ÷ area. Gas pressure comes from molecules hitting the container walls.

\[1\,\text{atm} = 760\,\text{mmHg} = 760\,\text{torr} = 101.325\,\text{kPa}\]
LawHeld constantRelationshipEquation
Boylen, TV ∝ 1/PP₁V₁ = P₂V₂
Charlesn, PV ∝ TV₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
Gay-Lussacn, VP ∝ TP₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
AvogadroP, TV ∝ nV₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂
\[\text{Combined gas law: } \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}\]

Temperatures in gas laws must be in kelvin. Using °C gives wrong answers (and can give negative volumes).

WorkedWorked example: Charles's law

A balloon holds 2.50 L at 25 °C. What is its volume at 100 °C (same pressure)?

\[V_2 = V_1\frac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.50\times\frac{373}{298} = 3.13\,\text{L}\]

WorkedWorked example: Boyle's law

4.0 L of gas at 1.0 atm is squeezed to 2.0 atm at constant temperature. V₂ = (1.0 × 4.0) / 2.0 = 2.0 L.

checks.x: Boyle's law: V ∝ 1/P.

o: Volume and pressure are proportional to absolute temperature
SI units must always be used

sections.title: The ideal gas equation
sections.html:
\[PV = nRT\]
R valueUse with
0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)P in atm, V in L
8.314 J/(mol·K)P in Pa, V in m³ (or energy work)

STP is 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atm. At STP, 1 mol of an ideal gas takes up 22.4 L.

WorkedWorked example: moles of gas

How many moles are in 5.00 L of gas at 25 °C and 1.20 atm?

\[n = \frac{PV}{RT} = \frac{1.20\times5.00}{0.08206\times298} = 0.245\,\text{mol}\]

Density and molar mass

\[d = \frac{PM}{RT} \qquad M = \frac{dRT}{P}\]

Heavier gases are denser: CO₂ (44 g/mol) is denser than air (≈ 29 g/mol), so it sinks.

Gas stoichiometry

Use PV = nRT to turn a gas volume into moles, then the mole ratio as in topic 10. Example: 2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂. 1.00 mol KClO₃ gives 1.50 mol O₂, which at STP is 1.50 × 22.4 = 33.6 L.

checks.q: At STP, 2.00 mol of an ideal gas occupies:
Which value of R goes with P in atm and V in L?
At the same T and P, which gas is densest?
checks.x: d = PM/RT, so the gas with the largest molar mass (44 g/mol) is densest.

sections.title: Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory
sections.html:
Dalton's law of partial pressures

\[P_\text{total} = P_A + P_B + \dots \qquad P_A = \chi_A P_\text{total},\ \ \chi_A = \frac{n_A}{n_\text{total}}\]

Collecting a gas over water: the gas is mixed with water vapour, so Pgas = Ptotal − Pwater (look up Pwater at that temperature).

WorkedWorked example: mole fraction

A mixture has 1.0 mol N₂ and 3.0 mol O₂ at 2.0 atm total. χ(O₂) = 3.0/4.0 = 0.75, so P(O₂) = 0.75 × 2.0 = 1.5 atm.

Kinetic molecular theory

  1. Gas particles are tiny compared with the distances between them (their own volume is negligible).
  2. They move constantly and randomly in straight lines.
  3. Collisions are elastic (no energy lost overall).
  4. There are no attractions or repulsions between particles.
  5. Average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.
\[u_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} \quad (R = 8.314,\ M \text{ in kg/mol})\]

Effusion: Graham's law

\[\frac{\text{rate}_A}{\text{rate}_B} = \sqrt{\frac{M_B}{M_A}}\]

Lighter gases effuse faster. H₂ (2 g/mol) effuses √(32/2) = 4 times faster than O₂ (32 g/mol).

Real gases stop behaving ideally at high pressure (particle volume matters) and low temperature (attractions matter).

checks.q: A mixture of 2.0 mol He and 2.0 mol Ar is at 3.0 atm. The partial pressure of He is:
How many times faster does H₂ effuse than O₂?
Gases behave least ideally at:
o: Low pressure and low temperature only
checks.x: Squeezed, cold particles take up real space and attract each other.

sections.title: Light and electromagnetic radiation
sections.html:
Light is an electromagnetic wave. Wavelength (λ) and frequency (ν) are linked by the speed of light:

\[c = \lambda\nu,\quad c = 3.00\times10^8\,\text{m/s}\]

Light also comes in packets of energy called photons:

\[E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda},\quad h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,\text{J·s}\]

Shorter wavelength = higher frequency = more energy. Order of increasing energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red → violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

WorkedWorked example: green light

λ = 500 nm = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m.

\[\nu = \frac{3.00\times10^8}{5.00\times10^{-7}} = 6.00\times10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\]
\[E = (6.626\times10^{-34})(6.00\times10^{14}) = 3.98\times10^{-19}\,\text{J per photon}\]

Per mole of photons: × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.40 × 10⁵ J = 240 kJ/mol.

The photoelectric effect

Light shining on a metal knocks out electrons only if each photon has enough energy (above a threshold frequency). Brighter light gives more electrons but not faster ones. This showed that light behaves as particles.

Convert nm to m (× 10⁻⁹) before using c = λν.

checks.q: Which has the highest energy per photon?
checks.x: UV has the shortest wavelength of these, so the highest energy.

checks.q: If the wavelength of light doubles, the energy of each photon:
checks.x: E = hc/λ, so E is inversely proportional to λ.

checks.q: Light of λ = 600 nm has frequency:

sections.title: The Bohr model and atomic spectra
sections.html:
Heated gases give off light at only certain wavelengths: a line spectrum. Bohr explained this for hydrogen: the electron can only have certain energies (energy levels n = 1, 2, 3 …).

\[E_n = -2.18\times10^{-18}\,\text{J}\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\]
  • n = 1 is the ground state (lowest energy). Higher n are excited states.
  • Emission: the electron drops to a lower level and gives out a photon. Absorption: it takes in a photon and jumps up.
\[\Delta E = 2.18\times10^{-18}\,\text{J}\left(\frac{1}{n_\text{f}^2}-\frac{1}{n_\text{i}^2}\right)\ \text{(size of the photon's energy)}\]

WorkedWorked example: n = 3 → n = 2

\[\Delta E = 2.18\times10^{-18}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) = 3.03\times10^{-19}\,\text{J}\]
\[\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^{8})}{3.03\times10^{-19}} = 6.56\times10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 656\,\text{nm}\]

That is the red line in hydrogen's visible (Balmer) series. Visible lines are drops to n = 2.

Beyond Bohr

  • de Broglie: moving particles have a wavelength, λ = h / mv.
  • Heisenberg uncertainty principle: you cannot know an electron's exact position and momentum at the same time. So we talk about orbitals (regions of probability), not fixed orbits.
  • The Bohr model only works for one-electron species (H, He⁺, Li²⁺).

checks.q: Which electron transition in hydrogen emits the highest-energy photon?
checks.x: The biggest drop in energy is to n = 1 from a high level. n = 2 → 3 is absorption, not emission.

checks.q: Visible lines in hydrogen's spectrum come from electrons falling to:
checks.x: This is the Balmer series. Falls to n = 1 are ultraviolet.

checks.q: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle says:
o: Position and momentum of an electron can't both be known exactly
Electrons move in fixed circular orbits
No two electrons have the same four quantum numbers
Light behaves only as a wave
checks.x: This is why electrons are described by orbitals (probabilities).

checks.x: l must be less than n, so n = 2 can only have l = 0 or 1.

sections.title: Electron configurations
sections.html:
The three rules

  • Aufbau principle: fill the lowest-energy orbitals first.
  • Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most 2, with opposite spins.
  • Hund's rule: in orbitals of equal energy (e.g. the three 2p), put one electron in each, with parallel spins, before pairing.

Filling order

1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p

Follow the periodic table: s-block (Groups 1–2), p-block (13–18), d-block (transition metals), f-block (lanthanides and actinides).

ElementFullNoble-gas shorthand
O (8)1s² 2s² 2p⁴[He] 2s² 2p⁴
Na (11)1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹[Ne] 3s¹
Fe (26)1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶[Ar] 4s² 3d⁶
Br (35)… 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵[Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵

Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ and Cu is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. Half-full and full d subshells are extra stable.

  • Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell (highest n). For main-group elements this matches the group: O has 6, Br has 7.
  • Orbital diagram for N: 1s ↑↓ 2s ↑↓ 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ (three unpaired electrons, by Hund's rule).

checks.q: The electron configuration of Cu is:
checks.x: Cu is an exception: a full 3d¹⁰ is more stable.

checks.q: How many unpaired electrons does an oxygen atom have?
checks.x: 2p⁴: ↑↓ ↑ ↑. Two are unpaired.

checks.q: Which orbital fills straight after 4s?
checks.x: The order is 4s then 3d then 4p.

sections.title: Periodic trends
sections.html:
Effective nuclear charge (Zeff) is the pull of the nucleus that outer electrons actually feel after shielding by inner electrons. It increases across a period, and that drives most trends.

PropertyAcross a period (→)Down a group (↓)Why
Atomic radiusDecreasesIncreasesHigher Zeff pulls electrons in; down a group, more shells
Ionisation energyIncreasesDecreasesElectrons held more tightly across; further from nucleus going down
Electron affinity (energy released)Generally more negativeGenerally less negativeNucleus attracts an added electron more strongly
ElectronegativityIncreasesDecreasesSame reasoning as ionisation energy; F is the highest
Metallic characterDecreasesIncreasesMetals lose electrons easily

Small atoms top right (F, Ne) have high ionisation energy and electronegativity. Large atoms bottom left (Cs, Fr) are the most metallic.

Ionisation energy exceptions: B < Be (B's 2p electron is easier to remove than a 2s) and O < N (O's paired 2p electron is pushed off by repulsion).

Successive ionisation energies

Each electron removed costs more. There is a huge jump once you start removing core electrons: for Mg, IE₃ is much larger than IE₂, which shows Mg has 2 valence electrons.

checks.q: Which atom has the largest radius?
checks.x: K is lowest in Group 1 here, with an extra shell.

checks.q: Which has the highest first ionisation energy?
checks.x: Noble gases at the top right hold their electrons most tightly.

checks.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of O lower than that of N?
o: O's 4th 2p electron is paired and repelled
O has a smaller nuclear charge
O has a full p subshell
checks.x: In O one 2p orbital holds two electrons, and their repulsion makes one easier to remove.

sections.title: Ions: configurations, sizes and magnetism
sections.html:
Electron configurations of ions

  • Main-group ions usually reach a noble-gas configuration: Na⁺ and O²⁻ are both [Ne] (they are isoelectronic).
  • Transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, then 3d: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.

Fill 4s before 3d, but remove 4s before 3d too. Writing Fe²⁺ as [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴ is a classic mistake.

Ion sizes

  • Cations are smaller than their atoms (fewer electrons, often a whole shell lost).
  • Anions are larger than their atoms (extra electron repulsion).
  • In an isoelectronic series, more protons means a smaller ion: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 electrons).

Magnetism

  • Paramagnetic: has unpaired electrons, attracted to a magnet (O₂, Fe³⁺ with 5 unpaired).
  • Diamagnetic: all electrons paired, slightly repelled (Zn²⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰, Ne).

This links straight into bonding (topics 24–28): ions with noble-gas configurations make ionic bonds, and valence electrons make Lewis structures.

checks.q: The electron configuration of Fe³⁺ is:
checks.x: Remove the two 4s electrons first, then one 3d: [Ar] 3d⁵.

checks.q: Which ion is smallest?
checks.x: All have 10 electrons; Mg²⁺ has the most protons (12), so it pulls hardest.

checks.q: Which species is diamagnetic?
checks.x: Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰: every electron is paired.

sections.title: Drawing a Lewis structure
sections.html:
1. Count all valence electrons. Add one for each negative charge, subtract one for each positive charge.
  2. Draw the skeleton: the least electronegative atom goes in the centre (never H, which only makes one bond).
  3. Join each outer atom to the centre with a single bond (2 electrons each).
  4. Give outer atoms lone pairs until each has an octet (H needs only 2).
  5. Put any electrons left over on the central atom.
  6. If the central atom has fewer than 8, turn outer lone pairs into double or triple bonds.
  7. Work out formal charges and pick the structure with the lowest ones.

Octet exceptions

  • Expanded octet: atoms in period 3 or below (P, S, Cl, Xe) can hold more than 8 electrons because they have empty d orbitals. Examples: PCl₅ (10 e⁻ on P), SF₄, SO₃, SOCl₂.
  • Period 2 atoms (C, N, O, F) can never go above 8: they only have 2s and 2p orbitals.

checks.q: How many valence electrons are in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻?
checks.x: N has 5, each O has 6 (18), plus 1 for the negative charge: 5 + 18 + 1 = 24.

checks.q: How many valence electrons are in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
checks.x: S 6 + O 4 × 6 = 24, plus 2 for the 2− charge: 32.

checks.q: Which atom is never the central atom in a Lewis structure?
checks.x: H can only make one bond, so it is always on the outside.

sections.title: Formal charge
sections.html:
\[\text{FC} = \text{valence e}^- - \tfrac12(\text{bonding e}^-) - \text{lone-pair e}^-\]

Quick version: FC = valence electrons − number of bonds − number of lone electrons.

  • The formal charges in a structure always add up to the overall charge (0 for a molecule, −1 for NO₃⁻).
  • No Lewis structure is complete without formal charges.
  • The most stable structure has formal charges of zero on as many atoms as possible.
  • If a negative charge is needed, it should sit on the most electronegative atom.

WorkedWorked example: NO₃⁻ (24 electrons; one N=O, two N–O)

Atom Valence e⁻ Bonds Lone e⁻ Formal charge
N 5 4 0 +1
O (double bond) 6 2 4 0
O (single bond) × 2 6 1 6 −1 each

Check: +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1, which matches the ion's charge.

WorkedWorked example: SOCl₂ (26 electrons)

  • Octet structure (S–O single): S = +1, O = −1.
  • Expanded octet (S=O double): S = 0, O = 0, so this one is more stable.

checks.q: What is the formal charge on N in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
checks.x: FC = 5 valence − 4 bonds − 0 lone electrons = +1. It matches the ion's charge.

checks.q: An O atom has one single bond and three lone pairs. Its formal charge is:
checks.x: FC = 6 − 1 bond − 6 lone electrons = −1.

checks.q: Which Lewis structure is the most stable?
o: The one with zero formal charge on as many atoms as possible
The one where every atom has an octet, whatever the charges
The one with the most double bonds
The one with the negative charge on the least electronegative atom
checks.x: Lowest formal charges win; a needed negative charge belongs on the most electronegative atom.

sections.title: Resonance
sections.html:
• Resonance happens when more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn by moving electrons only, never atoms.
  • Draw each form and join them with a double-headed arrow (↔).
  • The real molecule is a hybrid (average) of all the forms. It does not flip between them.
  • In NO₃⁻ there are three equivalent forms. All three N–O bonds are really the same length, between a single and a double bond, and the −1 charge is shared over the three O atoms.
  • Other examples from the notes: SO₃, SOCl₂ (forms A and B), HNO₂, SO₂Cl₂.

checks.q: Resonance structures of the same ion differ only in:
checks.x: You may move electrons, never atoms.

checks.q: What are the three N–O bonds in the real nitrate ion like?
o: All the same length, between a single and a double bond
One double and two single, fixed
Flipping between double and single very fast
checks.x: The real ion is a hybrid (average) of the three forms; it does not flip between them.

sections.title: VSEPR theory
sections.html:
Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other, so they spread out as far apart as possible to keep repulsion low.

Step by step

  1. Draw the Lewis structure.
  2. Count the electron regions on the central atom. A lone pair is one region, and a single, double or triple bond each count as one region.
  3. The number of regions gives the electron-pair geometry (EPG).
  4. The number of lone pairs gives the molecular geometry (the shape of the atoms only).

If there are no lone pairs, EPG and molecular geometry are the same. If there are lone pairs, they are different.

Memory aid: repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair. Lone pairs take more room, so they squeeze bond angles smaller: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O about 104.5°.

Where lone pairs go

  • Trigonal bipyramidal (5 regions): lone pairs go in equatorial positions.
  • Octahedral (6 regions) with 2 lone pairs: they go opposite each other.

Shapes table

3 0 Trigonal planar Trigonal planar 120° BF₃
3 1 Trigonal planar Bent under 120° SO₂

4 2 Tetrahedral Bent about 104.5° H₂O
5 0 Trigonal bipyramidal Trigonal bipyramidal 90°, 120° PCl₅

checks.x: A single, double or triple bond each counts as one region.

checks.q: H₂O has 4 electron regions and 2 lone pairs on O. Its molecular geometry is:
checks.x: The electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral, but the shape of the atoms alone is bent (about 104.5°).

checks.q: Why is the H–N–H angle in NH₃ 107° and not 109.5°?
o: The lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly
checks.x: Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair–bonding pair, so the bonds are squeezed together.

sections.title: Molecular polarity and dipole moments
sections.html:
• A polar bond forms when two atoms have different electronegativities. The more electronegative atom gets δ−, the other δ+.
  • A dipole moment measures how far the charge is separated (charge × distance). It has a direction, drawn as an arrow from δ+ to δ−.
  • The overall dipole moment of a molecule is the sum of its bond dipoles, taking direction into account.
  • Polar bonds do not always mean a polar molecule. If the shape is symmetrical and the outer atoms are all the same, the bond dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar.

Quick test

  1. Are there lone pairs on the central atom? Usually polar (NH₃, H₂O, SF₄). Exceptions are shapes that stay symmetrical, like square planar XeF₄ or linear XeF₂.
  2. Are the outer atoms different? Usually polar (CHCl₃).
  3. No lone pairs on the centre and all outer atoms the same? Non-polar (CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄, PCl₅, SF₆).
Molecule Shape Polar?
CO₂ Linear No, dipoles cancel
H₂O Bent Yes
BF₃ Trigonal planar No, dipoles cancel
NH₃ Trigonal pyramidal Yes
CCl₄ Tetrahedral No, dipoles cancel
CHCl₃ Tetrahedral (mixed atoms) Yes
SF₄ Seesaw Yes
XeF₄ Square planar No, dipoles cancel

Yes, because its bonds are polar

No, because C=O bonds are non-polar
checks.x: Polar bonds do not always mean a polar molecule; the shape decides.

checks.q: Which of these molecules is polar?
checks.x: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but one C–H and three C–Cl bonds differ, so the dipoles do not cancel.

checks.q: A dipole-moment arrow is drawn:
o: from the central atom outwards always
checks.x: The arrow points towards the more electronegative (δ−) end.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.html:
• Counting a double bond as two electron regions. It is one.
  • Forgetting the extra electron(s) for a negative ion.
  • Giving a period 2 atom (N, O, C) more than 8 electrons.
  • Mixing up EPG and molecular geometry: lone pairs count for EPG but not for the shape name.
  • Calling a molecule polar just because it has polar bonds. Check the shape first.

qs.q: Using FC = (valence e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻) − (lone e⁻), calculate the formal charge on every atom in one Lewis structure of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻. Show that the formal charges add up to the charge on the ion.
qs.ans:
Structure: N in the centre, one N=O and two N–O single bonds.
N: 5 − ½(8) − 0 = +1
Double-bonded O: 6 − ½(4) − 4 = 0
Each single-bonded O: 6 − ½(2) − 6 = −1 (two of them)
Sum: +1 + 0 − 1 − 1 = −1 = the charge on the ion.

qs.q: Draw all the resonance structures of NO₃⁻. In one or two sentences, explain what resonance means and what the real structure of the ion looks like.
qs.ans: Three equivalent structures, with the N=O double bond on a different O each time. Resonance means no single Lewis structure describes the ion. The real ion is a hybrid (average) of the three: all three N–O bonds are identical, between single and double, and the −1 charge is spread over the three O atoms.

qs.q: Thionyl chloride, SOCl₂, has S as the central atom. (a) Draw a Lewis structure in which every atom obeys the octet rule (S–O single bond). (b) Draw a second structure in which S has an expanded octet (S=O). (c) Calculate the formal charges on S and O in both, and say which is more stable and why.
qs.ans:
26 valence electrons.
(a) S single-bonded to O, Cl and Cl; one lone pair on S, three on O, three on each Cl.
(b) S=O, two S–Cl; one lone pair on S, two on O; S has 10 electrons.
(c) (a): S = 6 − 3 − 2 = +1, O = 6 − 1 − 6 = −1. (b): S = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, O = 6 − 2 − 4 = 0. Cl is 0 in both. (b) is more stable because every atom has a formal charge of zero.

qs.q: Draw the Lewis structure of SO₃ and explain why S may have more than eight electrons around it while N in NO₃⁻ may not.
qs.ans: 24 valence electrons. Lowest formal charges: three S=O double bonds, two lone pairs on each O, none on S; every formal charge is 0. (The octet form with one S=O and two S–O, with three resonance structures, is also accepted if formal charges are shown.) S is in period 3 with empty 3d orbitals, so it can hold more than 8 electrons; N is in period 2 with only 2s and 2p, so it is limited to 8.

qs.q: State the order of electron-pair repulsions from strongest to weakest. Use it to explain why the H–N–H angle in NH₃ is 107° and not 109.5°.
qs.ans: Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair. NH₃ has four regions (three bonds + one lone pair), so the electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (109.5°). The lone pair takes more room and repels the bonding pairs more strongly, pushing the N–H bonds together, so the angle shrinks to 107°.

qs.q: What is a dipole moment? Explain how a molecule can contain polar bonds and still be non-polar overall.
qs.ans: A dipole moment measures how far positive and negative charge are separated (charge × distance). It comes from a difference in electronegativity and points from δ+ to δ−. A molecule with polar bonds is non-polar when its shape is symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel and the total is zero (for example CO₂).

qs.q: Say whether each molecule is polar or non-polar, with a one-line reason from its shape: CO₂, H₂O, BF₃, NH₃, CCl₄, CHCl₃, SF₄.
qs.ans:
CO₂ non-polar: linear, C=O dipoles cancel.
H₂O polar: bent, dipoles do not cancel.
BF₃ non-polar: trigonal planar and symmetrical.
NH₃ polar: trigonal pyramidal because of the lone pair.
CCl₄ non-polar: tetrahedral with four identical bonds.
CHCl₃ polar: tetrahedral, but one C–H and three C–Cl differ.
SF₄ polar: the seesaw shape is not symmetrical.

qs.q: What is the first ionisation energy of an element?
o: The energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions
The energy released when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons
The energy needed to remove all the electrons from one mole of atoms
The energy needed to remove one electron from one mole of solid atoms
qs.x: Key words: one mole, gaseous atoms, one electron each, forming 1+ ions.

qs.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
qs.x: Ionisation energies are always for gaseous species, and the electron is removed, not added.

qs.q: Which equation represents the SECOND ionisation energy of magnesium?
qs.x: The second IE removes one electron from the 1+ ion. Mg(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻ is the sum of the first and second IEs, not the second alone.

qs.q: What are the usual units of ionisation energy?
qs.x: Energy per mole of electrons removed.

qs.q: Is ionisation endothermic or exothermic?

qs.x: The electron is attracted to the nucleus, so pulling it away always needs energy. IE values are always positive.

The distance of the outer electron from the nucleus
qs.x: Neutrons carry no charge, so they do not change the attraction on the outer electron.

qs.q: How does first ionisation energy generally change across a period from left to right?
o: It increases, then decreases after group 14
qs.x: Nuclear charge rises, the electrons go into the same shell (similar shielding) and the atoms get smaller, so the outer electron is held more tightly.

qs.q: How does first ionisation energy change down a group?
qs.x: The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is easier to remove, even though the nuclear charge is larger.

qs.q: Which of these has the HIGHEST first ionisation energy?
qs.x: Down group 1 the outer electron is further away and more shielded: Li 520 > Na 496 > K 419 kJ mol⁻¹.

qs.q: Which element has the highest first ionisation energy of all?

qs.q: Which element in period 3 has the highest first ionisation energy?

qs.sub: Trends across a period and down a group

qs.q: Which has the larger first ionisation energy, Na or Mg?
qs.x: Mg has one more proton with the outer electron in the same shell (Mg 738, Na 496 kJ mol⁻¹).
qs.sub: Trends across a period and down a group

qs.q: Which has the LOWER first ionisation energy, K or Ca?
qs.x: K has one fewer proton for a 4s electron in the same shell (K 419, Ca 590 kJ mol⁻¹).
qs.sub: Trends across a period and down a group

qs.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of Ar higher than that of Cl?
o: Ar has one more proton, and its outer electron is in the same shell with similar shielding
Ar's outer electron is in a new shell
Ar is a gas and Cl is not
qs.x: Same shell, more protons: a greater attraction on the outer electron.
qs.sub: Trends across a period and down a group

qs.q: Down group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba), the first ionisation energy:
qs.x: Atoms get larger and more shielded, so Be is highest and Ba lowest.
qs.sub: Trends across a period and down a group

qs.q: Across a period, the main reason ionisation energy rises is that:
o: the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons increases
qs.x: Protons are added but the extra electrons go into the same shell, which shields poorly, so the outer electrons feel a bigger pull.

qs.q: Why do group 1 metals react so readily to form 1+ ions?
o: Their first ionisation energies are low
Their first ionisation energies are high
qs.x: One electron alone in a new outer shell, far from the nucleus and well shielded, is easy to remove.

qs.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron LOWER than that of beryllium?
o: B loses an electron from the 2p subshell, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s electrons
B has fewer protons than Be
B's electron is removed from a paired orbital
B has a full outer shell
qs.x: Be loses a 2s electron; B loses a 2p electron. The 2p electron is further from the nucleus on average and shielded by 2s², so less energy is needed (B 801, Be 899).

qs.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen LOWER than that of nitrogen?
o: In O, the electron is removed from a 2p orbital holding a pair, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove
O has fewer protons than N
O's outer electron is in a higher shell
qs.x: N is 2p³, one electron in each orbital. O is 2p⁴, so one orbital holds a pair, and that pair repels (O 1314, N 1402).

qs.q: Put Be, B and C in order of increasing first ionisation energy.
qs.x: B 801 < Be 899 < C 1086 kJ mol⁻¹: B dips below Be because of the 2p electron.

qs.q: Put N, O and F in order of increasing first ionisation energy.
qs.x: O 1314 < N 1402 < F 1681 kJ mol⁻¹: O dips below N because of the paired 2p electrons.

qs.q: Why does each successive ionisation energy of an atom get larger?
o: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so the attraction on the remaining electrons is greater
The nucleus gains protons each time
The electrons move further from the nucleus
qs.x: Same number of protons, fewer electrons: the remaining electrons are held more tightly and the ion gets smaller.

qs.x: The big jump comes after the 3rd electron, so there are 3 outer electrons. This is aluminium.

qs.q: An element's first four ionisation energies are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10540 kJ mol⁻¹. Which group is it in?

qs.x: The huge jump after the 1st electron means only one outer electron. This is sodium.

qs.q: What causes a very large jump between two successive ionisation energies?
o: The next electron is removed from an inner shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded
The next electron is removed from the same subshell
The atom has gained a proton
A paired electron is being removed
qs.x: A jump marks the start of a new, inner shell.

qs.q: Element X shows a large jump between its 4th and 5th ionisation energies. What is the formula of its oxide?
qs.x: Four outer electrons put X in group 14, so it forms X⁴⁺ and the oxide XO₂.

qs.q: Why is the second ionisation energy of sodium much larger than its first?
o: The second electron comes from the full 2p subshell, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded
The second electron is in the 3p subshell
Na⁺ has fewer protons than Na
qs.x: Na is [Ne]3s¹. After the 3s electron goes, the next one is in the n = 2 shell.

qs.x: Same electron arrangement, but Mg²⁺ has the most protons (12), so its electrons are held most tightly.
