qs.x: H(g) → H⁺(g) + e⁻ is ionisation, and H⁺ + e⁻ → H is the reverse of ionisation.

qs.q: Which equation represents the SECOND electron affinity of oxygen?
qs.x: The second EA adds one electron to the 1− ion.

qs.q: What are the usual units of electron affinity?
qs.x: Energy per mole. Electronegativity is the one with no units (Pauling scale).

qs.q: A first electron affinity is given as −349 kJ mol⁻¹. What does the negative sign mean?
o: The value is below zero kelvin
qs.x: Negative ΔH means energy is given out as the electron is attracted in.

qs.q: Electron affinities are measured for atoms in which state?
qs.x: Gaseous, so that only the single isolated atom is involved.

qs.q: The first electron affinity of X equals, in size, the energy for which process (with the opposite sign)?
qs.x: Removing the extra electron from X⁻ is the exact reverse of adding it to X.

qs.q: Why are most first electron affinities exothermic?
o: The incoming electron is attracted by the nucleus of the neutral atom
The atom loses energy by losing an electron
The electron repels the other electrons
qs.x: The positive nucleus pulls on the incoming electron, so energy is released.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Why is every second electron affinity endothermic?
o: The electron is being added to a negative ion, which repels it
The ion has too many protons
The electron goes into an inner shell
qs.x: Energy must be put in to force an electron onto an ion that is already negative.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: For oxygen, first EA = −141 and second EA = +798 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the overall energy change for O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g)?
qs.x: Add them: −141 + 798 = +657 kJ mol⁻¹. Making O²⁻ from O is endothermic overall; oxides form because of the lattice energy released later.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Which process is endothermic?
qs.x: Any second electron affinity is endothermic.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Which group has first electron affinities close to zero or positive (unfavourable)?
qs.x: A new electron would have to start a new shell, far from the nucleus and well shielded.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Why is the electron affinity of beryllium or magnesium not favourable (about zero or positive)?
o: Their ns subshell is full, so the new electron must enter a higher-energy p subshell
qs.x: Be is 2s² and Mg is 3s²: the added electron goes into the empty p subshell.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Why is the electron affinity of nitrogen close to zero, much less favourable than carbon's?
o: N's 2p³ is half-filled, so the new electron must pair up and is repelled
N has fewer protons than C
N's new electron enters the 3s subshell
qs.x: C (2p²) accepts an electron into an empty 2p orbital (−122). N must pair an electron, so its EA is about 0.
qs.sub: Sign of first and second electron affinities

qs.q: Which element has the most exothermic first electron affinity of ALL elements?
qs.x: Cl −349 kJ mol⁻¹ is more negative than F −328.

qs.q: Why is fluorine's first electron affinity LESS exothermic than chlorine's?
o: F is very small, so its 2p electrons are crowded and repel the incoming electron
F has more protons than Cl
F's new electron enters a new shell
F is less electronegative than Cl
qs.x: High electron density in F's small 2p shell repels the new electron, outweighing the closer distance to the nucleus.

qs.q: Which shows the same small-atom effect as F and Cl?
o: O and S: S has the more exothermic first EA
N and P: N is far more exothermic
Na and K: K is more exothermic
He and Ne: He is more exothermic
qs.x: S (−200) is more exothermic than O (−141) for the same reason: O's small 2p shell is crowded.

qs.q: Arrange the halogens in order of INCREASINGLY exothermic first electron affinity.
qs.x: I −295, Br −325, F −328, Cl −349 kJ mol⁻¹. Cl is the most exothermic; F is out of order because it is so small.

qs.q: From Cl to I, how does the first electron affinity change?
qs.x: Larger atoms and more shielding mean a weaker pull on the incoming electron.

qs.q: Generally, across a period from group 1 to group 17, first electron affinity:
qs.x: Nuclear charge increases and atoms shrink, so the incoming electron is attracted more strongly (with dips at groups 2, 15 and 18).

qs.q: Which element has the more exothermic first electron affinity: carbon or nitrogen?
qs.x: C −122 kJ mol⁻¹; N is about 0 because of its half-filled 2p subshell.

qs.q: Which element has the more exothermic first electron affinity: oxygen or fluorine?
qs.x: F (−328) is one electron short of a full shell and has a higher nuclear charge than O (−141).

qs.q: Which statement about the first electron affinity of sodium (−53 kJ mol⁻¹) is correct?
o: It is slightly exothermic, but Na loses electrons far more readily than it gains them
It is the most exothermic in period 3
It equals the first ionisation energy of Na
qs.x: Group 1 atoms can accept a second s electron, so the value is small and negative.

qs.q: Why do halogens have the most exothermic first electron affinities in their periods?
o: They are one electron short of a full outer shell and have the highest nuclear charge of the non-noble elements in the period
They have the lowest ionisation energies
qs.x: The added electron completes the octet and is strongly attracted.

qs.q: Which atom will gain an electron with the most energy released?
qs.x: Cl −349. Ar and Mg have unfavourable EAs, and N's is about 0.

qs.q: Electron affinity differs from electronegativity because:
o: EA is a measured energy for an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity is an atom's pull on shared electrons in a bond
they are exactly the same thing
electronegativity has units of kJ mol⁻¹
qs.x: Two ideas with similar trends but different meanings.

qs.q: Which pair has the more exothermic first electron affinity listed FIRST?
qs.x: Li (−60) accepts an electron into 2s; Be's 2s is full, so its value is about zero or positive.

qs.q: Which element in period 3 has the most exothermic first electron affinity?
qs.x: Cl (−349) is one electron short of a full shell; Ar's value is unfavourable.

qs.q: Why is chlorine's first electron affinity more exothermic than sulfur's?
o: Cl has one more proton and the incoming electron enters the same shell
S has a full outer shell
Cl's new electron enters a new shell
qs.x: Greater nuclear charge, similar shielding: Cl −349, S −200 kJ mol⁻¹.

qs.q: Which of these atoms has a first electron affinity that is NOT exothermic?
qs.x: Neon's added electron would have to start the n = 3 shell.

sets.title: VSEPR shapes
sets.desc: 33 questions from counting regions to every shape, ions and bond angles.

qs.q: In VSEPR, what counts as one electron region (electron domain)?
o: A lone pair, a single bond, a double bond or a triple bond
qs.x: Any bond, single or multiple, counts as ONE region, and so does each lone pair.

qs.q: How many electron regions are there around S in SF₄?
qs.x: 4 S–F bonds + 1 lone pair = 5 regions.

qs.q: How many lone pairs are on Xe in XeF₄?
qs.x: Xe 8 valence electrons: 4 used in Xe–F bonds, 4 left = 2 lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the electron-pair geometry of NH₃?
qs.x: 4 regions (3 bonds + 1 lone pair) give a tetrahedral EPG. Trigonal pyramidal is the molecular shape.

qs.q: A molecule is AX₂E₂ (2 bonds, 2 lone pairs on the central atom). What is its shape?
qs.x: Like H₂O: tetrahedral EPG, bent molecule.

qs.q: Why do lone pairs make bond angles smaller?
o: Lone pairs are held closer to the central atom and repel more strongly than bonding pairs
Lone pairs count as two regions
Lone pairs make the atom smaller
qs.x: Repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair.

qs.q: Put the bond angles in order: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O.
qs.x: 109.5° > 107° > about 104.5°: each extra lone pair squeezes the angle.

qs.q: What is the shape of BeCl₂?
qs.x: 2 regions, no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of CO₂?
qs.x: Two C=O double bonds = 2 regions, no lone pairs on C.

qs.q: What is the shape and bond angle of BF₃?
qs.x: 3 regions, no lone pairs on B.

qs.q: What is the shape of SO₂?
qs.x: 3 regions on S (2 bonds + 1 lone pair): trigonal planar EPG, bent shape.

qs.q: What is the shape of SO₃?
qs.x: 3 regions on S, no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻?
qs.x: N has 3 regions and no lone pairs (the double bond counts as one region).

qs.q: What is the shape of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
qs.x: 3 regions on C, no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻?
qs.x: N has 2 bonding regions + 1 lone pair: bent (about 115°).

qs.q: What is the shape and bond angle of CH₄?
qs.x: 4 regions, no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of PCl₃?
qs.x: 4 regions on P (3 bonds + 1 lone pair), like NH₃.

qs.q: What is the shape of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
qs.x: 4 bonds and no lone pair on N.

qs.q: What is the shape of the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺?
qs.x: O has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair, like NH₃ (about 107°).

qs.q: What is the shape of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
qs.x: 4 regions around S and no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of PCl₅ and which bond angles does it have?
qs.x: 5 regions, no lone pairs: 3 equatorial at 120°, 2 axial at 90°.

qs.q: What is the shape of SF₄?
qs.x: 5 regions (4 bonds + 1 lone pair). The lone pair sits equatorial.

qs.q: What is the shape of ClF₃?
qs.x: 5 regions (3 bonds + 2 lone pairs, both equatorial).

qs.q: In ClF₃, where are the two lone pairs?
qs.x: Equatorial positions have more room, so lone pairs go there first.

qs.q: What is the shape of XeF₂?
qs.x: 5 regions (2 bonds + 3 equatorial lone pairs), leaving the two F atoms at 180°.

qs.q: What is the shape of the triiodide ion, I₃⁻?
qs.x: The central I has 2 bonds + 3 lone pairs = 5 regions, like XeF₂.

qs.q: What is the shape and bond angle of SF₆?
qs.x: 6 regions, no lone pairs.

qs.q: What is the shape of BrF₅?
qs.x: 6 regions (5 bonds + 1 lone pair).

qs.q: What is the shape of XeF₄?
qs.x: 6 regions (4 bonds + 2 lone pairs opposite each other).

qs.q: What is the shape of ICl₄⁻?
qs.x: Central I: 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 6 regions, like XeF₄.

qs.q: What is the shape of PF₆⁻?
qs.x: 6 bonding regions, no lone pairs on P.

qs.q: Which molecule has a 180° bond angle even though its central atom has lone pairs?
qs.x: The three lone pairs sit equatorially, so the two F atoms are directly opposite.

qs.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though its central atom has lone pairs?
qs.x: Square planar is symmetrical, so the four Xe–F dipoles cancel.

sets.title: Test papers: multiple choice
sets.desc: All 80 multiple-choice questions from your four test papers, each with its working.

qs.q: A sealed container holds nitrogen gas and liquid ethanol. Which statement is correct?
o: The system contains two substances in two different phases
The system is a pure compound
The system contains only one phase because both substances are fluids
The system is a homogeneous pure substance
qs.x: N₂ is a gas and ethanol is a liquid: two substances, two phases.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: A graduated cylinder reading is 35.60 mL with an uncertainty of ±0.05 mL. What is the percentage uncertainty?
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: A rectangular metal sample is 2.50 cm × 3.00 cm × 4.00 cm and has a mass of 270.0 g. What is its density?
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: Which conversion factor is needed to convert 0.0250 m³ into cm³?
An atom has 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons. What is its correct representation?
qs.x: Mass number = 26 + 30 = 56. Charge = 26 − 23 = +3. 26 protons is iron.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: Which pair consists of isotopes of the same element?
qs.x: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) and different mass numbers.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: What is the correct name of Cu(NO₃)₂?
qs.x: Two NO₃⁻ ions balance Cu²⁺, so copper is +2. NO₃⁻ is nitrate (NO₂⁻ is nitrite).

qs.q: Which substance is most appropriately classified as a molecular compound?
qs.x: PCl₃ is made of two non-metals sharing electrons. The others are metal + non-metal ionic compounds.

qs.q: A substance contains 52.2% carbon, 13.0% hydrogen and 34.8% oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 2.0 mol of nitrogen reacts with 5.0 mol of hydrogen. Which statement is correct?
o: Both reactants are present in exact stoichiometric proportions
qs.x: 2.0 mol N₂ needs 3 × 2.0 = 6.0 mol H₂, but only 5.0 mol is there, so H₂ runs out first.

qs.q: Which combination produces a precipitate when the aqueous solutions are mixed?
qs.x: Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂(s), a yellow precipitate. All the other products are soluble (nitrates, Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts).
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species undergoes reduction?
qs.x: Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons to become Cu: gain of electrons is reduction. Zn is oxidised.

qs.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl in enough water to make 500.0 mL? (NaCl = 58.5 g mol⁻¹)
A gas is heated from 250 K to 400 K at constant pressure. Its initial volume is 2.50 L. What is its final volume?
qs.x: Charles's law: V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.50 × 400/250 = 4.00 L.
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas occupies 4.00 L at 27 °C and 100 kPa. What volume will it occupy at 127 °C and 150 kPa?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas mixture has a total pressure of 800 mmHg. The mole fraction of carbon dioxide is 0.15. What is its partial pressure?
qs.x: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total = 0.15 × 800 = 120 mmHg.
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Which radiation has the shortest wavelength?
qs.x: Order of decreasing wavelength: microwaves > infrared > ultraviolet > X-rays.

qs.q: A photon has a wavelength of 400 nm. What is its energy? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
Which electron configuration represents Fe²⁺? (Fe = 26)
qs.x: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Transition metals lose the 4s electrons first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶.

qs.q: Which element has the highest first ionisation energy?
qs.x: Ne is a noble gas with a full shell and the highest nuclear charge for its shell among these. Na, Mg and Al lose an electron from n = 3.

qs.q: A pure substance melts and then boils. Which statement correctly describes these changes?
o: Both are physical changes involving changes in intermolecular arrangement
Both are chemical changes involving bond formation
Melting is chemical while boiling is physical
Both processes change the chemical identity of the substance
qs.x: Only the arrangement of particles changes; the substance stays the same.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: A balance reads 8.425 g with an uncertainty of ±0.015 g. What is the percentage uncertainty?
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: A cube has a mass of 64.0 g and a volume of 8.00 cm³. What is its density?
qs.x: 64.0 ÷ 8.00 = 8.00 g cm⁻³. Both data have 3 significant figures, so the answer has 3 (8.000 has 4).
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: A student measures a length of 4.50 cm. What is this in metres?
Which statement correctly distinguishes atomic number from mass number?
o: Atomic number is the number of protons, while mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons
Atomic number is the total number of protons and neutrons, while mass number is the number of electrons
Atomic number is the number of neutrons, while mass number is the number of protons
Atomic number is the number of electrons, while mass number is the number of neutrons
qs.x: Z = protons. A = protons + neutrons.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: An element has isotopes of mass 24.0 u, 25.0 u and 26.0 u with abundances 79%, 10% and 11%. What is the average atomic mass?
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: What is the correct formula for ammonium phosphate?
qs.x: NH₄⁺ is 1+ and PO₄³⁻ is 3−, so three ammonium ions balance one phosphate.

qs.q: Which compound contains a transition metal in the +2 oxidation state?
qs.x: CoCl₂: Co is +2. CoCl₃: +3. Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇: +6. Mn in KMnO₄: +7.

qs.q: A compound contains 43.6% phosphorus and 56.4% oxygen. What is its empirical formula? (P = 31.0; O = 16.0)
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: How many molecules are in 0.250 mol of CO₂?
Which reaction is a precipitation reaction?
qs.x: Two aqueous ions form an insoluble solid. The others are neutralisation, redox and dissolving.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: In 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻, which species is the oxidising agent?
qs.x: Cl₂ gains electrons (is reduced) and so oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺. The oxidising agent is the species that is reduced.

qs.q: A student prepares 250.0 mL of solution containing 0.0500 mol of solute. What is its concentration?
A gas has a pressure of 95.0 kPa at 300 K. What is its pressure at 450 K if the volume stays constant?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas occupies 5.00 L at 100 kPa and 300 K. What is its volume at 150 kPa and 450 K?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas mixture contains 3.0 mol helium and 2.0 mol argon at a total pressure of 500 kPa. What is the partial pressure of helium?
qs.x: Mole fraction of He = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60. 0.60 × 500 = 300 kPa.
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Which statement correctly relates photon energy and frequency?
o: Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency
Photon energy is inversely proportional to frequency
Photon energy is independent of frequency
Photon energy is directly proportional to wavelength
qs.x: E = hf. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

qs.q: A source emits photons with a frequency of 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the energy per photon? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
What is the ground-state electron configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
qs.x: Cr is an exception: a half-filled 3d⁵ with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s².

qs.q: Which statement explains the general trend in atomic radius across Period 3 from Na to Cl?
o: Atomic radius generally decreases because effective nuclear charge increases
Atomic radius generally increases because additional electron shells are occupied
Atomic radius remains constant because all elements have the same number of shells
Atomic radius decreases because nuclear charge decreases
qs.x: Same number of shells, more protons: the electrons are pulled in closer.

qs.q: A sample contains ice, liquid water and dissolved sodium chloride. Which classification best describes it when all three are in the same container?
o: A heterogeneous mixture containing more than one phase
A pure compound because water is chemically unchanged
A homogeneous mixture consisting of a single phase
A pure element containing three physical states
qs.x: Salt water is one liquid phase and ice is a separate solid phase, so the sample is a mixture with two phases: heterogeneous.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: A metal block has a mass of 48.62 g and a volume of 6.25 cm³. What is its density to the correct number of significant figures?
qs.x: 48.62 ÷ 6.25 = 7.7792. The volume has 3 significant figures, so round to 3: 7.78 g cm⁻³.
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: A balance gives 12.486 g with an uncertainty of ±0.003 g. What is the percentage uncertainty?
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: Convert 72.0 km h⁻¹ into m s⁻¹.
A neutral atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 37. Which describes its subatomic particles?
qs.x: Protons = Z = 17; neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20; neutral, so electrons = 17.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: An element has two isotopes: ⁶³X (69.2%) and ⁶⁵X (30.8%). What is its average atomic mass?
qs.x: (63 × 0.692) + (65 × 0.308) = 43.60 + 20.02 = 63.62 u. It is nearer 63 because that isotope is more common.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: Which formula represents iron(III) sulfate?
qs.x: Fe³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: the lowest common multiple of the charges is 6, so 2 Fe³⁺ and 3 SO₄²⁻. FeSO₄ is iron(II) sulfate.

qs.q: Which compound contains the greatest number of oxygen atoms per formula unit?
qs.x: Al₂(SO₄)₃: 3 × 4 = 12 O. Ca(NO₃)₂: 6. Na₂CO₃: 3. Mg(OH)₂: 2.

qs.q: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.33% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula?
qs.x: C 40.0 ÷ 12.01 = 3.33, H 6.67 ÷ 1.008 = 6.62, O 53.33 ÷ 16.00 = 3.33. Ratio 1 : 2 : 1. C₂H₄O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆ have this composition but are molecular formulas, not the simplest ratio.
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. If 5.40 g of Al reacts with 10.65 g of Cl₂, which reactant is limiting? (Al = 27.0; Cl = 35.5)
qs.x: Al: 5.40 ÷ 27.0 = 0.200 mol. Cl₂: 10.65 ÷ 71.0 = 0.150 mol. 0.200 mol Al needs 0.200 × 3/2 = 0.300 mol Cl₂, but only 0.150 mol is there, so Cl₂ runs out first.

qs.q: Equal volumes of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃ and 0.20 mol dm⁻³ NaCl are mixed. Which net ionic equation represents the reaction?
qs.x: Only the ions that form the precipitate appear. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
What volume of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is needed to completely neutralise 25.0 mL of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄?
A gas occupies 2.40 L at 100 kPa. At constant temperature, the pressure rises to 160 kPa. What is its new volume?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas sample contains 0.50 mol at 300 K and 100 kPa. What volume does it occupy? (R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
A mixture contains 2.0 mol nitrogen and 1.0 mol oxygen at a total pressure of 300 kPa. What is the partial pressure of oxygen?
qs.x: Mole fraction of O₂ = 1.0/3.0. × 300 = 100 kPa.
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Which electromagnetic radiation has the highest energy per photon?
qs.x: Gamma rays have the highest frequency, and E = hf.

qs.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom moves from n = 4 to n = 2. Which statement describes this transition?
o: Energy is emitted as a photon
Energy is absorbed from a photon
The electron remains at the same energy level
qs.x: Moving to a lower level releases the energy difference as light (here the blue-green Balmer line, 486 nm).
qs.group: 19. The Bohr model and atomic spectra

qs.q: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT allowed for an electron in an atom?
qs.x: l can only go from 0 to n − 1. For n = 2, l = 2 is impossible.

qs.q: Which species has the largest ionic radius?
qs.x: All four have 18 electrons. S²⁻ has the fewest protons (16), so its electrons are held least tightly.

qs.q: A mixture of sand and sodium chloride is stirred into water. After filtration and evaporation of the filtrate, which statement correctly describes the separation?
o: Sand is retained during filtration, while sodium chloride is recovered by evaporation
Sodium chloride is retained during filtration, while sand evaporates
Both substances pass through the filter and are separated by distillation
Sand dissolves while sodium chloride remains insoluble
qs.x: NaCl dissolves and passes through the filter; insoluble sand stays on the filter paper. Evaporating the filtrate leaves the salt.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: A thermometer records 28.45 °C with an uncertainty of ±0.10 °C. What is the percentage uncertainty?
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: A liquid has a mass of 45.75 g and occupies 50.0 mL. What is its density to three significant figures?
qs.x: 45.75 ÷ 50.0 = 0.915 g mL⁻¹. 50.0 has 3 significant figures, so the answer has 3.
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: Which expression has the dimensions (SI units) of energy?
qs.x: Energy = force × distance = (kg m s⁻²) × m = kg m² s⁻² (the joule). kg m s⁻¹ is momentum, kg m⁻¹ s⁻² is pressure.
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: An ion contains 15 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons. Which species is it?
qs.x: 15 protons is phosphorus. Mass number = 15 + 16 = 31. Charge = 15 − 18 = −3.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: An element is 75% isotope X-10 and 25% isotope X-11. What is its average atomic mass?
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: What is the correct name for N₂O₅?
qs.x: Molecular compounds use prefixes for both elements: di- for 2 N, penta- for 5 O.

qs.q: Which ionic compound needs the greatest number of chloride ions per formula unit?
qs.x: Al³⁺ needs three Cl⁻ to balance its charge; Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ need two; Na⁺ needs one.

qs.q: A compound contains 27.3% carbon, 4.55% hydrogen and 68.15% oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
qs.x: C 27.3 ÷ 12.01 = 2.27, H 4.55 ÷ 1.008 = 4.51, O 68.15 ÷ 16.00 = 4.26. Divide by 2.27: about 1 : 2 : 1.9, so CH₂O₂. (The paper's data is slightly rough, but CH₂O₂ is the only close option; CH₂O and C₂H₄O₂ would be 40% carbon.)
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: In 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, how many moles of oxygen are produced from 4.00 mol of KClO₃?
qs.x: Ratio KClO₃ : O₂ = 2 : 3. 4.00 × 3/2 = 6.00 mol.

qs.q: Which net ionic equation represents the reaction between an acid and a strong base?
qs.x: In neutralisation the spectator ions cancel, leaving H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

qs.q: In MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ under acidic conditions, how many electrons are gained by manganese?
qs.x: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2: a gain of 5 electrons.

qs.q: A student dilutes 25.0 mL of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl to 250.0 mL. What is the final concentration?
A gas at 27 °C occupies 3.00 L. What volume will it occupy at 127 °C at constant pressure?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A gas has a volume of 10.0 L at 200 kPa and 300 K. What volume will it occupy at 100 kPa and 450 K?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: A container holds 0.25 mol helium and 0.75 mol neon. What is the mole fraction of helium?
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Which statement about the photoelectric effect supports the particle nature of light?
o: Electrons are emitted only when the incident light frequency exceeds a threshold frequency
Increasing light intensity always increases the kinetic energy of emitted electrons
Light energy is transferred continuously regardless of frequency
The wavelength of light determines the number of electrons in an atom
qs.x: Each photon carries E = hf. Below the threshold frequency no single photon has enough energy, however bright the light.

qs.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron travelling at 2.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
Which subshell can hold a maximum of 10 electrons?
qs.x: A d subshell has 5 orbitals × 2 = 10. s holds 2, p holds 6, f holds 14.

qs.q: Which element is expected to have the largest atomic radius?
qs.x: Radius increases down a group (K has 4 shells) and decreases across a period, so K is largest.

sets.title: Test papers: Section B
sets.desc: The 16 Section B calculations from your test papers, with the working for each part.

qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas
qs.q:
A sample of a compound contains 2.40 g of carbon, 0.40 g of hydrogen and 3.20 g of oxygen.
(a) Calculate the moles of carbon. (2)
(b) Calculate the moles of hydrogen atoms. (2)
(c) Determine the empirical formula. (2)
(d) The compound is completely combusted: C₂H₄O₂ + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the volume of oxygen at STP needed to combust 0.100 mol of the compound, using 22.4 L mol⁻¹. (4)
steps: (d) From the equation given, 1 mol of compound needs 2 mol O₂. 0.100 mol needs 0.200 mol O₂.
qs.hint: Divide each mass by its molar mass. For (d), read the mole ratio of O₂ to the compound straight from the equation the paper gives.

qs.q:
A 20.0 mL sample of sulfuric acid is completely neutralised by 32.0 mL of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
(a) Calculate the moles of NaOH used. (2)
(b) Calculate the moles of H₂SO₄ neutralised. (2)
(c) Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid. (3)
(d) Identify the type of reaction. (1)
(e) State the number of moles of water produced. (2)
qs.ans: (a) 8.00 × 10⁻³ mol (b) 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol (c) 0.200 mol dm⁻³ (d) neutralisation (e) 8.00 × 10⁻³ mol

qs.q:
Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). A 25.0 g sample of CaCO₃ is heated. (CaCO₃ = 100.0 g mol⁻¹; CaO = 56.0 g mol⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the initial moles of calcium carbonate. (2)
(b) Calculate the theoretical moles of calcium oxide produced. (2)
(c) Calculate the theoretical mass of calcium oxide. (3)
(d) If the actual mass obtained is 11.2 g, calculate the percentage yield. (3)

A 25.0 mL sample of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HCl is completely neutralised by NaOH. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O
(a) Calculate the moles of HCl present. (2)
(b) Calculate the moles of NaOH needed. (2)
(c) If 20.0 mL of NaOH is needed, calculate its concentration. (3)
(d) Identify the spectator ions in the net ionic neutralisation equation. (3)
steps: (d) Full ionic: H⁺ + Cl⁻ + Na⁺ + OH⁻ → Na⁺ + Cl⁻ + H₂O. Net ionic: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). Spectators: Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
qs.ans: (a) 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol (b) 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol (c) 0.250 mol dm⁻³ (d) Na⁺ and Cl⁻

qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory
qs.q:
A vessel of volume 8.00 L contains 0.40 mol of hydrogen gas and 0.60 mol of nitrogen gas at 350 K. (R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the total number of moles. (1)
(b) Calculate the total pressure of the mixture. (3)
(c) Calculate the mole fraction of hydrogen. (2)
(d) Calculate the partial pressure of nitrogen. (2)
(e) Which gas diffuses faster, hydrogen or nitrogen? (2)
steps: (e) Hydrogen: by Graham's law, rate ∝ 1/√M, and H₂ (2.02 g mol⁻¹) is much lighter than N₂ (28.0 g mol⁻¹), about 3.7 times faster.

qs.q:
An electron travels at 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. The mass of an electron is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
(a) Calculate its momentum. (2)
(b) Calculate its de Broglie wavelength, using h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (3)
(c) State the maximum number of electrons in the n = 3 level. (2)
(d) State the maximum number of electrons in a single p subshell. (1)
(e) State the number of orbitals in a d subshell. (2)

A 0.250 mol sample of an ideal gas occupies 5.00 L at 300 K. (R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the pressure in kPa. (3)
(b) The gas is compressed to 2.50 L at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure. (2)
(c) A second gas has a molar mass of 64.0 g mol⁻¹; the first has 16.0 g mol⁻¹. Calculate the ratio of the effusion rate of the first gas to the second. (3)
(d) Name the law relating effusion rates and molar masses. (2)
steps: (b) Boyle's law: half the volume, double the pressure: 124.7 × 5.00/2.50 = 249 kPa
(c) rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁) = √(64.0/16.0) = √4 = 2: the first gas effuses twice as fast.

qs.q:
A compound contains 5.60 g of iron and 2.40 g of oxygen.
(a) Calculate the moles of iron. (2)
(b) Calculate the moles of oxygen atoms. (2)
(c) Determine the empirical formula. (2)
(d) The compound reacts with carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron produced from 16.0 g of Fe₂O₃. (4)
steps: 1 Fe₂O₃ gives 2 Fe, so n(Fe) = 0.200 mol. m = 0.200 × 55.85 = 11.2 g

qs.q:
A 25.0 mL sample of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ BaCl₂ is mixed with 40.0 mL of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄. BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
(a) Calculate the moles of BaCl₂ present. (2)
(b) Calculate the moles of Na₂SO₄ present. (2)
(c) Identify the limiting reactant. (2)
(d) Calculate the theoretical mass of BaSO₄ formed (BaSO₄ = 233.4 g mol⁻¹). (4)
steps: (c) The ratio is 1 : 1 and BaCl₂ is the smaller amount, so BaCl₂ is limiting.

qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory
qs.q:
A gas mixture contains 0.40 mol of nitrogen and 0.10 mol of oxygen in a 10.0 L container at 300 K. (R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the total moles. (1)
(b) Calculate the mole fraction of oxygen. (2)
(c) Calculate the total pressure using the ideal gas equation. (3)
(d) Calculate the partial pressure of oxygen. (2)
(e) At the same temperature, which effuses faster, nitrogen or oxygen? (2)
steps: (e) Nitrogen: N₂ (28.0 g mol⁻¹) is lighter than O₂ (32.0 g mol⁻¹), so by Graham's law it effuses faster (√(32/28) = 1.07 times).

qs.q:
Consider sulfur (S), atomic number 16.
(a) Write its complete electron configuration. (2)
(b) State the number of unpaired electrons in the ground-state atom. (2)
(c) State the number of occupied electron shells. (1)
(d) Write the electron configuration of S²⁻. (2)
(e) Explain the difference in size between S and S²⁻. (3)
steps: (b) 3p⁴ fills as ↑↓ ↑ ↑ (Hund's rule), so 2 unpaired electrons.
(e) S²⁻ is larger. It has the same 16 protons but 18 electrons, so electron–electron repulsion increases and each electron feels less pull from the nucleus; the electron cloud spreads out.
qs.ans: (a) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴ (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (e) S²⁻ is larger: same protons, more electrons, more repulsion.

qs.q:
Consider the molecule NH₃.
(a) State the number of valence electrons in the molecule. (1)
(b) State the number of bonding electron pairs around nitrogen. (2)
(c) State the number of lone pairs on nitrogen. (2)
(d) Identify the electron-domain geometry. (2)
(e) Identify the molecular geometry. (2)
(f) Explain why the H–N–H bond angle is smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle. (1)
steps: (e) Only atoms count for the shape: trigonal pyramidal
(f) The lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, squeezing the angle from 109.5° to about 107°.
qs.ans: (a) 8 (b) 3 (c) 1 (d) tetrahedral (e) trigonal pyramidal (f) lone pair–bond pair repulsion is stronger, so about 107°

qs.q:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. A student reacts 4.80 g Mg with 100.0 mL of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl. (Mg = 24.0 g mol⁻¹; R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the initial moles of magnesium. (2)
(b) Calculate the initial moles of HCl. (2)
(c) Identify the limiting reactant. (2)
(d) Calculate the moles of hydrogen gas produced. (2)
(e) Calculate the volume of hydrogen at 300 K and 100 kPa. (2)
steps: (c) 0.200 mol Mg would need 0.400 mol HCl, but only 0.100 mol is there: HCl is limiting.
qs.hint: Compare what each reactant needs using the 1 : 2 ratio.

qs.q:
In acidic solution, permanganate ions oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions.
(a) State the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻. (1)
(b) State the oxidation number of manganese in Mn²⁺. (1)
(c) State the number of electrons gained by each manganese atom. (2)
(d) State the number of electrons lost by each Fe²⁺ ion. (1)
(e) Write the balanced overall ionic equation in acidic solution. (5)
steps: (e) Half-equations: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (× 5).
Add them: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Check charge: left −1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right +2 + 15 = +17 ✓
qs.hint: Balance O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with electrons. Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 so the electrons cancel.

qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory
qs.q:
A container of volume 12.0 L contains 0.50 mol of oxygen and 1.50 mol of nitrogen at 300 K. (R = 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
(a) Calculate the total moles. (1)
(b) Calculate the mole fraction of oxygen. (2)
(c) Calculate the total pressure. (3)
(d) Calculate the partial pressure of nitrogen. (2)
(e) Calculate the partial pressure of oxygen. (2)

Consider the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻.
(a) Calculate the total number of valence electrons. (2)
(b) State the number of equivalent resonance structures. (2)
(c) State the formal charge on nitrogen in a conventional resonance structure. (2)
(d) Identify the molecular geometry around nitrogen. (2)
(e) State the approximate O–N–O bond angle. (2)
steps: (b) The N=O double bond can sit on any of the three O atoms: 3
(c) N has 4 bonds and no lone pairs: FC = 5 − 4 − 0 = +1
(d) 3 electron domains, no lone pair on N: trigonal planar

sets.title: Past exams: multiple choice
sets.desc: 105 multiple-choice questions from the 2010, 2011, 2013, 2017 and 2019 final exams, each with its working.

qs.q: Which mixture consists of one element and one compound only?
o: An alloy of zinc and copper
qs.x: O₂ is an element and H₂O is a compound. O₂ + N₂ and Zn + Cu are two elements; NaCl + H₂O is two compounds.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: How many significant figures are in 15.0843 g, 0.996 g/mL and 25.00 mL respectively?
qs.x: 15.0843: all six digits count. 0.996: leading zero does not count, 3. 25.00: trailing zeros after the decimal point count, 4.
qs.group: 2. Measurement, SI units and significant figures

qs.q: Which species has 41 neutrons and 28 electrons?
qs.x: Ge: Z = 32, so neutrons = 73 − 32 = 41 and electrons = 32 − 4 = 28. ⁷¹Ga³⁺ has 28 electrons but 40 neutrons; ⁶⁸Zn²⁺ has 38 neutrons.
qs.group: 4. Atoms, isotopes and average atomic mass

qs.q: Which classification of an element is NOT correct?
o: Sr (Z = 38) is an alkaline earth metal
qs.x: Tin is a metal (group 14 below germanium). The metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te.
qs.group: 1. Matter and how it is classified

qs.q: Which name–formula pair is NOT correct?
qs.x: Copper(II) is Cu²⁺, which balances one SO₄²⁻: CuSO₄·5H₂O. Cu₂SO₄ would be copper(I) sulfate.

qs.q: A compound of nitrogen and oxygen only contains 36.85% N by mass. What is its empirical formula?
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: What coefficients balance __C₅H₁₂ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O?
qs.x: 5 C gives 5CO₂; 12 H gives 6H₂O. O on the right = 10 + 6 = 16 atoms = 8O₂.

qs.q: Classify H₂SO₃, CoSO₄ and C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ in water, in that order.
qs.x: H₂SO₃ (sulfurous acid) is a weak acid. CoSO₄ is a soluble salt: strong. Sucrose is a molecular non-acid: non-electrolyte.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: Which ion is a spectator ion in Ba(OH)₂(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l)?
qs.x: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ become the precipitate; H⁺ and OH⁻ become water. Every ion ends up in a product, so none is a spectator.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: Identify the reducing agent: Cu(s) + 4H⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ → Cu²⁺ + 2NO₂(g) + 2H₂O
qs.x: Cu goes from 0 to +2, so it is oxidised and is the reducing agent. N goes from +5 to +4 (reduced), so NO₃⁻ is the oxidising agent.

qs.q: Balance Cr₂O₇²⁻ → Cr³⁺ in acidic solution. Which statement is true?
o: There are 6 electrons on the left side
There are 7H₂O on the left side
There are 12H⁺ on the right side
There are 2Cr₂O₇²⁻ on the left side
qs.x: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Each Cr goes +6 → +3, two Cr gain 6 electrons.

qs.q: What volume of 18.0 M H₂SO₄ is needed to prepare 250 mL of 0.500 M H₂SO₄?
A gas has a pressure of 755 Torr at 27 °C in 250 mL. What is its pressure at −5 °C in 500 mL?
qs.group: 15. Pressure and the simple gas laws

qs.q: An unknown gas takes 44.3 s to effuse; Ne takes 30.0 s under the same conditions. What is the molar mass of the gas?
qs.x: Time is proportional to √M: M = 20.18 × (44.3/30.0)² = 44.0 g/mol. The slower gas is the heavier one.
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Blue light has λ = 470 nm. What is the energy of one mole of these photons?
The second Lyman line is the transition n = 3 → n = 1. What is its wavelength? (R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)
qs.group: 19. The Bohr model and atomic spectra

qs.q: Which statement about atomic orbitals is NOT true?
o: An atomic orbital is identified by four quantum numbers n, l, mₗ and mₛ
There are three p orbitals in a p subshell
mₗ is related to the orientation of an orbital
n is related to the energy and size of an orbital
qs.x: An orbital is fixed by n, l and mₗ. mₛ describes the electron's spin, not the orbital.

qs.q: Which set of quantum numbers is acceptable for an electron?
qs.x: l must be 0 … n − 1, mₗ a whole number from −l to +l, and mₛ = ±½. Only the n = 3, l = 0 set obeys all rules.

qs.q: What is the maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have n = 4?
How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state Ge atom (Z = 32) have?
qs.x: Ge = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p². By Hund's rule the two 4p electrons go into separate orbitals: 2 unpaired.

qs.q: Which has the largest radius: Br⁻, Kr, Rb⁺, Se²⁻, Sr²⁺?
qs.x: All have 36 electrons (isoelectronic). Se²⁻ has the fewest protons (34), so the electrons are held least tightly and it is largest.

qs.q: Arrange Al, O, P in order of increasing first ionisation energy.
qs.x: IE rises across a period and up a group. Al (left of period 3) < P (right of period 3) < O (period 2).

qs.q: How many lone pairs and bonding pairs are on the central atom in IF₇?
qs.x: Valence electrons = 7 + 7 × 7 = 56. Seven I–F bonds use 14; the 42 left fill the F atoms (6 each). Nothing remains on I.

qs.q: In the Lewis structure F–S=N, S carries one lone pair and N two lone pairs (F has three). What are the formal charges on F, S and N?
qs.x: FC = valence − lone electrons − ½ bonding. F: 7 − 6 − 1 = 0. S: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. N: 5 − 4 − 2 = −1.

qs.q: Electronegativities: H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5. Which bond is the most polar?
qs.x: ΔEN: O–H 1.4, N–H 0.9, O–C 1.0, C–H 0.4, O–N 0.5. The largest difference is the most polar bond.
qs.group: 30. Ionic bonding, bond polarity and lattice energy

qs.q: What is the molecular geometry of NF₃?
qs.x: N has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair: tetrahedral electron domains, so the molecule (atoms only) is trigonal pyramidal.

qs.q: A triple bond consists of
qs.x: The first bond between two atoms is always σ; every extra bond is π.

qs.q: In acetic acid CH₃–C(=O)–O–H, what are the approximate angles around the C=O carbon (angle 1) and around the O of O–H (angle 2)?
qs.x: The carbonyl C has 3 electron domains: trigonal planar, ≈120°. The O–H oxygen has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs: tetrahedral domains, ≈109.5° (a little less).

qs.q: What is the hybridisation of P in PCl₅?
qs.x: P has 5 bonding domains and no lone pairs: trigonal bipyramidal, which uses one s, three p and one d orbital: sp³d.

qs.q: The acceleration of a falling ball is 9.8 m s⁻². Express it in mm ms⁻².
A tanker carries 1095 L of petrol of density 0.75 kg L⁻¹. What mass of petrol is that, in grams?
Vitamin C is 40.92% C, 4.58% H and the rest oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula?
qs.group: 8. Percent composition, empirical and molecular formulas

qs.q: Balance __CH₃NH₂ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O + __N₂.
qs.x: 4CH₃NH₂ has 4 C, 20 H, 4 N → 4CO₂ + 10H₂O + 2N₂. O on the right = 8 + 10 = 18 = 9O₂.

qs.q: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What mass of O₂ reacts completely with 0.50 mol CH₄?
Which precipitate forms when Hg₂(NO₃)₂(aq) and KI(aq) are mixed?
qs.x: Mercury(I) is the diatomic ion Hg₂²⁺, so with I⁻ it gives Hg₂I₂, which is insoluble. Nitrates of K⁺ stay dissolved.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: Balance V²⁺(aq) → VO₂⁺(aq) in basic solution. Which statement is FALSE?
o: There are 6e⁻ on the left side
There are 4OH⁻ on the left side
There are 2H₂O on the right side
There are 3e⁻ on the right side
qs.x: V goes +2 → +5, losing 3e⁻: V²⁺ + 4OH⁻ → VO₂⁺ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻. Electrons are on the right, and there are 3, not 6.

qs.q: A mixture of 6.02 × 10²³ molecules NH₃ and 3.01 × 10²³ molecules H₂O has a total pressure of 6.00 atm. What is the partial pressure of NH₃?
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: Which increase when a gas is heated at constant volume? I pressure; II kinetic energy of molecules; III attractive forces between molecules
qs.x: Hotter molecules move faster (more KE) and hit the walls harder and more often (more pressure). Attractive forces do not increase.
qs.group: 17. Gas mixtures and kinetic molecular theory

qs.q: 50.0 mL of 0.100 M H₂SO₄ is mixed with 100.0 mL of 0.050 M NaOH and evaporated to dryness. What solid remains?
qs.x: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.00500 mol; n(NaOH) = 0.00500 mol. A 1 : 1 ratio removes only one H⁺: H₂SO₄ + NaOH → NaHSO₄ + H₂O.
qs.group: 13. Aqueous reactions, precipitation and net ionic equations

qs.q: What mass of CaBr₂ is needed for 250 mL of 0.500 M solution? (CaBr₂ = 199.9 g mol⁻¹)
20.0 g of Mg is added to 1.00 L of 1.00 M HCl (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂). Which is true?
qs.x: n(Mg) = 20.0 ÷ 24.31 = 0.823 mol, which needs 1.65 mol HCl. Only 1.00 mol HCl is present, so HCl runs out first.

qs.q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state scandium atom have?
qs.x: Sc = [Ar] 3d¹ 4s². The single 3d electron is unpaired.

qs.q: Which set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) could describe the highest-energy electron of a ground-state Ga atom?
qs.x: Ga = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p¹. The last electron is 4p: n = 4, l = 1, mₗ = −1, 0 or +1. mₗ = 1 with l = 0, or mₗ = 2 with l = 1, is impossible.

qs.q: Which change is a reduction?
qs.x: N goes 0 → −3 (gains electrons). C goes +2 → +4 and Mn +4 → +7 (oxidations); Cr stays +6.

qs.q: The mineral spinel is ionic and contains only Mg, Al and O. What is its simplest formula?
qs.x: Mg²⁺ + 2Al³⁺ = +8, balanced by 4O²⁻ = −8. The others do not sum to zero.

qs.q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 545 nm?
Which species is smallest?
qs.x: Removing all three valence electrons strips Ga's n = 4 shell; Ga³⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ and much smaller than any of the neutral atoms.

qs.q: Radio Botswana broadcasts at 89.9 MHz. What is the wavelength?
Chlorine is more likely than sodium to exist as an anion because
o: chlorine has a greater electron affinity than sodium
chlorine has a smaller ionisation energy than sodium
chlorine is more metallic than sodium
qs.x: Cl releases much more energy when it gains an electron (it then has a full octet). Cl is actually smaller, has a higher IE and is a non-metal.

qs.q: Which is an acceptable Lewis structure for SO₂ (18 valence electrons)?
o: O=S–O: one lone pair on S, two on the double-bonded O, three on the single-bonded O
O–S–O: single bonds only, two lone pairs on S, three on each O
O=S=O with no lone pair on S and two on each O
O≡S–O with no lone pair on S
qs.x: Count: O=S–O uses 6 bonding electrons + 2 + 4 + 6 lone = 18 ✓, and every atom has an octet. The single-bond version needs 20 electrons.

qs.q: How many bonding and lone pairs are on the central atom in SF₄?
qs.x: 34 valence electrons. Four S–F bonds use 8; 24 go on the F atoms; the last 2 are a lone pair on S.

qs.q: Which species must have an expanded octet?
qs.x: PCl₆⁻ has six P–Cl bonds: 12 electrons around P. A period-2 central atom can never exceed 8.

qs.q: In a BF₃ structure with one B=F double bond and two B–F single bonds, what are the formal charges on B, a single-bonded F and the double-bonded F?
qs.x: B: 3 − 0 − ½(8) = −1. Single F: 7 − 6 − 1 = 0. Double F: 7 − 4 − 2 = +1. (This is why the all-single-bond structure is preferred.)

qs.q: Which pair of atoms forms the most polar bond?
qs.x: The bond is most polar where the electronegativity gap is largest: F (4.0) and B (2.0) differ by 2.0.
qs.group: 30. Ionic bonding, bond polarity and lattice energy

qs.q: According to VSEPR theory, a molecule's geometry is the one in which
o: repulsion between valence electron pairs is at a minimum
repulsion between valence electron pairs is at a maximum
attraction between valence electron pairs is at a maximum
qs.x: Electron domains spread out as far as possible to minimise their mutual repulsion.

qs.q: Order the strength of electron-pair repulsions.
qs.x: Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only and spread out more, so they repel most.

qs.q: For ClF₃, what are the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry?
qs.x: Cl has 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 5 domains (trigonal bipyramidal). Lone pairs go equatorial, leaving a T shape: AB₃E₂.

qs.q: How many σ and π bonds are in CH₂=CH–CH₂–C(=O)–CH₃?
qs.x: C–H: 2 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8. C–C: 4. C=O: 1 σ. Total σ = 13. Each double bond (C=C, C=O) adds one π: 2 π.

qs.q: What is the molecular geometry of the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻?
qs.x: 26 electrons: S has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair (AB₃E). Electron domains tetrahedral, shape trigonal pyramidal.

qs.q: Which option pairs a pure substance with a chemical change?
o: Magnesium, and the corrosion of aluminium
Rice pudding, and the melting of ice
Sand, and crushing an aspirin tablet
Air, and an iron pin sticking to a magnet
qs.x: Magnesium is an element (pure). Corrosion makes a new substance (chemical change). Melting, crushing and magnetism are physical; pudding, sand and air are mixtures.

qs.q: Earth's oceans hold about 1.36 × 10⁹ km³ of water. What is this in litres?
qs.x: 1 km³ = (10³ m)³ = 10⁹ m³, and 1 m³ = 10³ L, so 1 km³ = 10¹² L. 1.36 × 10⁹ × 10¹² = 1.36 × 10²¹ L.

qs.q: Which ion formula/name pair is WRONG?
qs.x: S₂O₃²⁻ is thiosulfate. Sulfite is SO₃²⁻.

qs.q: Which nuclear symbol has 35 neutrons and 28 electrons?
qs.x: Cu: Z = 29, so 64 − 29 = 35 neutrons and 29 − 1 = 28 electrons. ⁶⁴Zn²⁺ has 34 neutrons; Ni²⁺ has 26 electrons.

qs.x: Acetic acid is weak, so it stays as molecules in the equation. Na⁺ is a spectator.

qs.x: With l = 0 the only allowed mₗ is 0, so (ii) is impossible. (i) and (iii) obey all the rules.

qs.x: In the ground state 4s fills before 3d, so the 19th electron should be 4s¹, not 3d¹.

o: H–C≡N with one lone pair on N
H=C=N with two lone pairs on N
H–C=N with one lone pair on C and two on N
H–C≡N with a lone pair on C
qs.x: 10 valence electrons: H–C (2) + C≡N (6) + lone pair on N (2). H keeps 2, C and N each have an octet.

qs.q: How many bonding and non-bonding pairs are around Xe in XeF₄?
qs.x: 36 electrons: 4 bonds (8) + 24 on F atoms leaves 4 = 2 lone pairs on Xe. Square planar.

qs.q: Which are chemical changes? (i) rusting of iron (ii) melting of butter (iii) decomposition of water by electricity (iv) boiling of alcohol
qs.x: Rusting and decomposition make new substances. Melting and boiling only change the state.

qs.x: l = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: s, p, d, f, g. (n² = 25 is the number of orbitals; 2n² = 50 electrons.)

qs.q: Arrange O, S, Mg and Ba in order of increasing atomic radius.
qs.x: Radius grows down a group (O < S) and leftward across a period (S < Mg in period 3). Ba (period 6) is largest.

qs.q: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of an element X?
qs.x: Each ionisation energy removes one electron from a gaseous species. The second starts from the 1+ ion.

qs.q: How many bonding pairs and lone pairs are on iodine in ICl₄⁻?
qs.x: 36 valence electrons (18 pairs). Four I–Cl bonds + 12 lone pairs on Cl = 16 pairs; 2 are left on I. AB₄E₂: square planar.

qs.q: Which molecule is T-shaped?
qs.x: Br has 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs (AB₃E₂): T-shaped. BCl₃ is trigonal planar; NCl₃ and PCl₃ are trigonal pyramidal.

qs.q: Which has the greater (more exothermic) first electron affinity, F or Cl, and why?
o: Cl, because F's small 2p shell is crowded and repels the added electron
F, because it is more electronegative
They are equal, being in the same group
qs.x: Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) beats F (−328 kJ mol⁻¹): the extra electron in tiny F feels strong repulsion from the other 2p electrons.

qs.q: A snail moves at 5.00 mm s⁻¹. What is this in pm µs⁻¹?

qs.q: An element has isotopes 37.919 u (5.07%), 39.017 u (15.35%) and 42.111 u (79.85%). What is its average atomic mass?
qs.x: 0.0507 × 37.919 + 0.1535 × 39.017 + 0.7985 × 42.111 = 1.922 + 5.989 + 33.626 = 41.54 u. It sits close to the most abundant isotope, as expected.

qs.q: Which element has the largest second ionisation energy: K, Ca, Sc or Ti?
qs.x: K⁺ is [Ar]: its second electron must come from the full n = 3 noble-gas core.

qs.q: What is the shape of XeF₄?
qs.x: Xe has 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs (AB₄E₂). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving the F atoms in a square.
